Can a BMS alone protect a battery? Littelfuse, the 'last safety component' that physically cuts off abnormal current | Littelfuse (NASDAQ: LFUS)
When asked what protects the safety of EVs and large-scale storage batteries, many people might think of a BMS (Battery Management System).
The BMS is the 'brain' that monitors voltage and temperature to detect abnormalities.
However, detecting an abnormality is not the same as reliably stopping dangerous current.
When a large current flows due to a short circuit or similar event, there is a final safety component that physically disconnects the circuit.
That is the fuse.
Hello everyone, this is MoneyGolem.
The company I am introducing this time, Littelfuse (NASDAQ: LFUS), is a US company that, true to its name, started with fuses and has expanded its business into semiconductors, sensors, relays, and contactors.
Fuses are small and usually appear to be doing nothing.
However, at the moment an accident occurs, they blow themselves to stop the current in order to protect the battery, wiring, inverter, and people.
Even in production technology, safety components cannot simply be 'good if they are cheap.' This is because it is necessary to prove through design and evaluation that they operate reliably during an abnormality and do not malfunction during normal operation.
This time, we will look at Littelfuse not just as a small component manufacturer, but as a company that sells 'physical safety devices' that are the last line of defense to stop abnormal current in battery systems.
1. What kind of company is Littelfuse?
Littelfuse is a circuit protection, power control, and sensing manufacturer founded in 1927.
The business is broadly divided into three areas: electronics, transportation, and industrial equipment.
Representative products are as follows:
Overvoltage protection components such as TVS diodes
Sensors for temperature, position, current, etc.
In the battery sector, we have touchpoints in EV battery packs, high-voltage power distribution units, onboard chargers, inverters, and stationary energy storage systems.
High-voltage DC fuses are a particularly clear example.
When battery cells are connected in series, the system voltage rises from several hundred volts to over 1,000V. The stored energy also increases, and in the event of a short circuit, a very large current can flow.
Littelfuse offers 1,000Vdc-rated fuses for EVs and products with a breaking capacity of 1,500Vdc and up to 250kA for battery storage systems.
As batteries grow into larger systems—from cells to modules, racks, and PCS—the importance of circuit protection also increases.
Littelfuse is not a battery manufacturing company.
However, we are a company that transforms the large energy stored in batteries into a state where it can be used safely.
2. Why is a fuse necessary if there is a BMS?
A BMS monitors the battery's voltage, current, temperature, and more.
When it detects an abnormality, it instructs the contactor to "cut the circuit."
So, is having a BMS and a contactor enough?
In actual safety design, we even consider cases where the control system does not function normally.
The sensor cannot correctly detect abnormal values
The control signal does not reach its destination
The contactor contacts weld shut and will not open
A short-circuit current exceeding expectations flows all at once
In such cases, the fuse melts its internal metal at a certain current level or higher, physically disconnecting the circuit.
In other words, if the BMS is the "brain that considers abnormalities," the fuse is the safety valve that finally cuts the current path.
Moreover, cutting high-voltage direct current is not easy.
While alternating current periodically approaches zero, direct current has no natural zero point. If arc discharge continues even after the inside of the fuse has melted, there is a possibility that the current cannot be safely interrupted.
Therefore, fuses are required to have the following design characteristics:
At what current and after how many seconds will it operate?
How large a short-circuit current can it interrupt?
Are its characteristics stable at both high and low temperatures?
Will it avoid malfunctioning during normal inrush current?
Can it provide protection before surrounding cables or contactors are damaged?
From the perspective of production technology and equipment design, what is important is not just 'breaking'.
It must break reliably, only when necessary, and at the intended time.
Replacing them with cheaper parts that lead to more malfunctions will result in equipment downtime. Conversely, if they fail to break during an abnormality, it leads to safety accidents.
To avoid both of these, fuses carry a humble yet heavy responsibility.
3. Why are small fuses difficult to replace?
Fuses look like simple components when viewed only by their appearance.
However, before adopting them for mass-produced products, it is necessary to verify voltage, normal current, inrush current, short-circuit current, ambient temperature, cooling conditions, cable capacity, etc., and design protection coordination.
Furthermore, safety tests, durability tests, and abnormality tests must be conducted on the actual equipment, and they must be registered in design drawings and bills of materials.
Compliance with application-specific standards, such as AEC-Q200 for automobiles and IEC or UL for energy storage systems, is also important.
When changing to a different manufacturer after mass production has started, it does not end with just a price comparison.
Verify breaking capacity and how the arc is contained
Review protection coordination with contactors and cables
Re-evaluate under different temperature conditions
Re-obtaining customer approvals and safety certifications
Even for small components, the scope of impact from a change extends to the entire system.
This is where Littelfuse's switching costs lie.
Furthermore, the company possesses a wide range of products, not just fuses, but also semiconductors, sensors, relays, and contactors.
Customers can consult collectively on where to place which protection components in a circuit. The failure modes, test data, and application-specific know-how accumulated over many years are also competitive advantages that are difficult to see in individual components alone.
On the other hand, these are not components consumed during normal production, like MEC's chemical solutions or DISCO's processing tools.
Demand for fuses generally arises when they operate during an abnormality or for maintenance and replacement.
Even so, as the mass production volume of automobiles and storage batteries increases, the installation demand accumulates for each model adopted.
Littelfuse's moat lies in not being consumed daily, but being difficult to remove once incorporated into a safety design.
We will look at the numbers from here.
At MoneyGolem, to standardize calculation methods across companies, we calculate FCF using the following formula:
FCF = Operating Cash Flow - Capital Expenditures
FY2021: Revenue $2.08 billion / FCF $283 million / FCF margin 13.6%
FY2022: Revenue $2.514 billion / FCF $315 million / FCF margin 12.5%
FY2023: Revenue $2.363 billion / FCF $371 million / FCF margin 15.7%
FY2024: Revenue $2.191 billion / FCF $292 million / FCF margin 13.3%
FY2025: Revenue $2.386 billion / FCF $366 million / FCF margin 15.3%
FCF was positive in all 5 periods. The total FCF margin for the 5 periods is approximately 14.1%.
While it is not an A-rated company that exceeds 20% growth every year, as a manufacturer of electronic and industrial components with cyclical business, we can confirm its stable cash-generating ability.
In fiscal year 2025, revenue increased by 8.9% year-on-year, operating cash flow was $434 million, and capital expenditure was $68 million.
On the other hand, the final net loss for the same fiscal year was $72 million.
The main reason is the $301 million goodwill impairment recorded in the electronics segment. Since this was an accounting loss that did not directly involve cash outflow, FCF remained positive even though net income was in the red.
This does not mean that you can rest easy just by looking at FCF.
Littelfuse is a company that has expanded its product lineup through acquisitions. If the acquired businesses do not earn as expected, goodwill impairment may occur again.
Along with cash-generating ability, it is necessary to confirm whether the funds used for acquisitions are generating sufficient profits.
A tailwind for Littelfuse is the electrification of society.
In EVs, stationary battery storage, renewable energy, and data centers, the power and DC voltage handled are increasing.
The higher the power, the greater the damage in the event of an abnormality, increasing the importance of circuit protection.
In the industrial equipment segment for fiscal year 2025, energy storage, renewable energy, data centers, and air conditioning-related sectors supported growth.
Littelfuse is not a company that bets on the popularity of finished products.
Its appeal lies in having a wide range of 'common safety components' that become necessary as the number of products using electricity increases.
On the other hand, there are risks that should be checked.
Cyclicality of electronics, automotive, and industrial equipment
If customer production volumes or capital investments decrease, demand for components also decreases. When inventory adjustments by distributors overlap, sales tend to fluctuate more than final demand.
While it can expand its product lineup, if businesses acquired at high prices do not grow, the return on investment will be delayed. The goodwill impairment in fiscal year 2025 is an important warning for looking at future capital allocation.
There are multiple specialized manufacturers for fuses and circuit protection. Furthermore, as electronic fuses and semiconductor-based protection technologies advance, the division of roles with mechanical and fusible components may change.
While there is a sense of stability in having positive FCF for five consecutive periods, the total FCF margin for those five periods is approximately 14.1%. It does not reach the 20% range, which is MoneyGolem's A-rating criteria.
It is important to consider the competitiveness as a safety component and the financial evaluation separately.

When asked what protects the safety of EVs and large-scale storage batteries, many people might think of a BMS (Battery Management System).
The BMS is the 'brain' that monitors voltage and temperature to detect abnormalities.
However, detecting an abnormality is not the same as reliably stopping dangerous current.
When a large current flows due to a short circuit or similar event, there is a final safety component that physically disconnects the circuit.
That is the fuse.
Hello everyone, this is MoneyGolem.
The company I am introducing this time, Littelfuse (NASDAQ: LFUS), is a US company that, true to its name, started with fuses and has expanded its business into semiconductors, sensors, relays, and contactors.
Fuses are small and usually appear to be doing nothing.
However, at the moment an accident occurs, they blow themselves to stop the current in order to protect the battery, wiring, inverter, and people.
Even in production technology, safety components cannot simply be 'good if they are cheap.' This is because it is necessary to prove through design and evaluation that they operate reliably during an abnormality and do not malfunction during normal operation.
This time, we will look at Littelfuse not just as a small component manufacturer, but as a company that sells 'physical safety devices' that are the last line of defense to stop abnormal current in battery systems.
1. What kind of company is Littelfuse?
Littelfuse is a circuit protection, power control, and sensing manufacturer founded in 1927.
The business is broadly divided into three areas: electronics, transportation, and industrial equipment.
Representative products are as follows:
Overvoltage protection components such as TVS diodes
Sensors for temperature, position, current, etc.
In the battery sector, we have touchpoints in EV battery packs, high-voltage power distribution units, onboard chargers, inverters, and stationary energy storage systems.
High-voltage DC fuses are a particularly clear example.
When battery cells are connected in series, the system voltage rises from several hundred volts to over 1,000V. The stored energy also increases, and in the event of a short circuit, a very large current can flow.
Littelfuse offers 1,000Vdc-rated fuses for EVs and products with a breaking capacity of 1,500Vdc and up to 250kA for battery storage systems.
As batteries grow into larger systems—from cells to modules, racks, and PCS—the importance of circuit protection also increases.
Littelfuse is not a battery manufacturing company.
However, we are a company that transforms the large energy stored in batteries into a state where it can be used safely.
2. Why is a fuse necessary if there is a BMS?
A BMS monitors the battery's voltage, current, temperature, and more.
When it detects an abnormality, it instructs the contactor to "cut the circuit."
So, is having a BMS and a contactor enough?
In actual safety design, we even consider cases where the control system does not function normally.
The sensor cannot correctly detect abnormal values
The control signal does not reach its destination
The contactor contacts weld shut and will not open
A short-circuit current exceeding expectations flows all at once
In such cases, the fuse melts its internal metal at a certain current level or higher, physically disconnecting the circuit.
In other words, if the BMS is the "brain that considers abnormalities," the fuse is the safety valve that finally cuts the current path.
Moreover, cutting high-voltage direct current is not easy.
While alternating current periodically approaches zero, direct current has no natural zero point. If arc discharge continues even after the inside of the fuse has melted, there is a possibility that the current cannot be safely interrupted.
Therefore, fuses are required to have the following design characteristics:
At what current and after how many seconds will it operate?
How large a short-circuit current can it interrupt?
Are its characteristics stable at both high and low temperatures?
Will it avoid malfunctioning during normal inrush current?
Can it provide protection before surrounding cables or contactors are damaged?
From the perspective of production technology and equipment design, what is important is not just 'breaking'.
It must break reliably, only when necessary, and at the intended time.
Replacing them with cheaper parts that lead to more malfunctions will result in equipment downtime. Conversely, if they fail to break during an abnormality, it leads to safety accidents.
To avoid both of these, fuses carry a humble yet heavy responsibility.
3. Why are small fuses difficult to replace?
Fuses look like simple components when viewed only by their appearance.
However, before adopting them for mass-produced products, it is necessary to verify voltage, normal current, inrush current, short-circuit current, ambient temperature, cooling conditions, cable capacity, etc., and design protection coordination.
Furthermore, safety tests, durability tests, and abnormality tests must be conducted on the actual equipment, and they must be registered in design drawings and bills of materials.
Compliance with application-specific standards, such as AEC-Q200 for automobiles and IEC or UL for energy storage systems, is also important.
When changing to a different manufacturer after mass production has started, it does not end with just a price comparison.
Verify breaking capacity and how the arc is contained
Review protection coordination with contactors and cables
Re-evaluate under different temperature conditions
Re-obtaining customer approvals and safety certifications
Even for small components, the scope of impact from a change extends to the entire system.
This is where Littelfuse's switching costs lie.
Furthermore, the company possesses a wide range of products, not just fuses, but also semiconductors, sensors, relays, and contactors.
Customers can consult collectively on where to place which protection components in a circuit. The failure modes, test data, and application-specific know-how accumulated over many years are also competitive advantages that are difficult to see in individual components alone.
On the other hand, these are not components consumed during normal production, like MEC's chemical solutions or DISCO's processing tools.
Demand for fuses generally arises when they operate during an abnormality or for maintenance and replacement.
Even so, as the mass production volume of automobiles and storage batteries increases, the installation demand accumulates for each model adopted.
Littelfuse's moat lies in not being consumed daily, but being difficult to remove once incorporated into a safety design.

Along with cash-generating ability, it is necessary to confirm whether the funds used for acquisitions are generating sufficient profits.
A tailwind for Littelfuse is the electrification of society.
In EVs, stationary battery storage, renewable energy, and data centers, the power and DC voltage handled are increasing.
The higher the power, the greater the damage in the event of an abnormality, increasing the importance of circuit protection.
In the industrial equipment segment for fiscal year 2025, energy storage, renewable energy, data centers, and air conditioning-related sectors supported growth.
Littelfuse is not a company that bets on the popularity of finished products.
Its appeal lies in having a wide range of 'common safety components' that become necessary as the number of products using electricity increases.
On the other hand, there are risks that should be checked.
Cyclicality of electronics, automotive, and industrial equipment
If customer production volumes or capital investments decrease, demand for components also decreases. When inventory adjustments by distributors overlap, sales tend to fluctuate more than final demand.
